title: Confidence-gated transaction categorization with accountant review of uncertain items
problem: Staff code bank and card transactions monthly for every client across different charts of accounts, and that coding sets the quality of every later report.
approach: A model proposes an account with a confidence score; high-confidence items post and uncertain ones go to an accountant for bulk review.
An independent field study associates AI use with a 7.5-day shorter monthly close and about 8.5% of accountant time reallocated (independent).
Digits' benchmark reports 97.8% accuracy for its ledger-native model versus 79.1% for outsourced accountants (vendor-published).
Intuit announced auto-categorization where only high-confidence items post; the accountant decides when to switch it on.

title: Bank, card and clearing-account reconciliation by AI matching with an exceptions list
problem: Reconciling bank, card and clearing accounts means exporting statements, maintaining fragile matching rules and hunting mismatches.
approach: Matching software ingests feeds, matches transactions without hand-built rules, finalizes clean reconciliations and presents a short, prioritized exceptions list.
An unnamed Top 100 firm's practice uses FloQast; monthly labor on project reconciliations fell from 8 hours to 5 (vendor-published).
The accountant clears the exceptions list; the job manager reviews and signs off the reconciliation checklist.
who: FloQast, Digits, an unnamed Top 100 firm

title: Agents prepare month-end close across a firm's clients; accountants approve and review
problem: Client accounting capacity is capped by headcount: each close needs categorization, reconciliation, exceptions, journal entries and statements for every client, and staff are scarce.
approach: Agent platforms such as Pilot's Meridian, Ramp's Stack and BlackLine's Verity Prepare prepare the close in the firm's existing ledgers.
BlackLine reports up to 92% less reconciliation preparation time; Basis reports 30% average savings (vendor-published).
A vendor benchmark of unattended agents found books over 15% off CPA baselines after several months.
The accountant approves the agent's plan and drafted entries before posting, and reviews finished books before client delivery.

title: Staff book entries via an AI ledger assistant, with locked-period approval
problem: Booking entries and reconciling a quarterly close by hand takes hours, and an agent that writes to the ledger needs real controls.
approach: Accountants use a general assistant connected to the ledger through Digits' Write MCP, shipped 13 October 2026.
Writes apply in open periods and queue for manager approval in locked periods; agents work within the user's permissions.
One AI-native practice reports two quarterly closes taking about 1 hour 40 minutes versus 7 by hand (vendor-published).

title: Continuous close and automated monthly packages on an AI-native ledger (solo firm)
problem: A small firm spent most of each month producing financials by exporting, cleaning, formatting and emailing statements client by client.
approach: Elev8 CFO moved clients to Digits and built a pipeline on its API that generates and delivers branded statements monthly.
Elev8 reports monthly close falling from 18 days to 5 (self-reported); Digits reports hours falling from about 108 to 20 (vendor-published).
A parallel close on a starter cohort came before cut-over; a review gate before automated release is not described.

title: AI-assisted live dashboards, variance explanations and management reporting for client advisory
problem: Static month-end packages arrive late, commentary comes late, and routine bookkeeping crowds out time for dashboards and explaining movements.
approach: Accountants use ledger-connected dashboards and assistants to spot unusual movements, drill into drivers, draft variance explanations and walk clients through live financials.
Small firms on Digits describe drill-down and screen-sharing live financials in meetings; no outcome is measured.
The accountant confirms each variance explanation against source records, and a manager reviews commentary before delivery.

title: Cash-flow forecasts, budgets and scenario planning built from live ledger data
problem: Fractional CFO clients want forward-looking cash-flow and budget views, which take time to assemble; advisory capacity is limited by data cleanup and staffing.
approach: Armanino built a 13-week cash-flow tool on robotic process automation, not generative AI, and reports client demand (self-reported, no figure).
Digits says firms use a general assistant on ledger data for 13-week forecasts and budgets; Intuit announced conversational answers and AI forecasts.
The adviser sets and reviews forecast and scenario assumptions before client delivery.

title: Fractional CFO drafting of technical memos, with retrieval over past memos
problem: Fractional CFO and controllership clients ask for technical accounting memos that take hours to write.
approach: Eventus Advisory Group turned its past memos into a retrieval index behind a memo-generator bot that produces a first draft.
Its head of AI research estimates time per memo falling from 4 hours to 30 minutes (self-reported).
A person reviews and corrects every draft, and the CFO owns the memos.

title: AI-accelerated onboarding, ledger migration and catch-up cleanup sold as projects
problem: New clients arrive with years of messy data, duplicates and unreconciled periods; cleanups took weeks and were often unprofitable.
approach: Firms use AI categorization and matching to bring books current in days, pricing cleanups as discrete projects or recurring quarterly engagements.
A small firm reports cleanup in 2 to 4 days (vendor-published); a solo firm migrated 27 clients in about 40 hours (self-reported).
The accountant approves the cleaning plan, reviews write-offs and opening balances, and runs a reconciliation check before go-live.

title: AP and bill-pay agents that code and route invoices, with fraud screening
problem: Accounts payable for client accounting involves manual invoice entry, coding, vendor emails and payment coordination, and firms paying bills face email fraud and deepfakes.
approach: AI-enabled AP tools such as BILL, Tipalti and Ramp extract invoice details, categorize expenses, match purchase orders, route approvals and schedule payments.
BILL states aggregates of 1,100-plus hours saved by a receipt agent and about 1,000 days by a tax-document agent (vendor-published).
The owner or adviser approves payments, and an accountant reviews coding exceptions. No client accounting firm reports AI fraud screening yet.

title: Payroll preparation with AI-guided workflows, anomaly flags and payroll journal entries
problem: Payroll prep means re-entering hours and deductions clients send by email and pulling the same reports after every run, client by client.
approach: Gusto (October 2026) lets accountants run payroll from one dashboard, with email-drafted inputs, change tracking and anomaly flags.
Intuit's Payroll Agent validates data; Ramp's Stack agent drafts the payroll entry; Pilot says its AI ties liabilities. No outcome figure.
The accountant reviews flagged anomalies and approves payroll changes and the entry before posting.

title: AI chasing of missing client documents and open questions inside the ledger
problem: Teams spend large amounts of time chasing documents and answers, and one solo firm says email follow-ups took clients 10 to 12 days to answer.
approach: Questions and answers move into the transaction feed or collaboration inbox, and AI chases missing documents, escalating judgment calls to an accountant.
Intuit says its collaboration inbox lets Intuit Intelligence chase follow-ups automatically.
One solo firm reports client response falling to a few business days, attributed to the platform rather than AI specifically (vendor-published).

title: Cross-client portfolio view of close status, open tasks and anomalies for managers
problem: A manager running dozens of clients cannot easily see which close is late or which client's expenses spiked.
approach: A portfolio view shows close status for every client; AI summarizes issues, alerts on anomalies and answers cross-client queries.
Examples are Intuit Accountant Suite cross-client insights (open beta, June 2026) and Ramp's Advisor Console. No outcome figure is published.
The manager decides what to act on.

title: In-house automation that scans, summarizes and tickets incoming vendor mail and invoices
problem: A small in-house accounting team was inundated with physical mail: vendor invoices, tax notices and statements.
approach: The Capital Area Food Bank controller built an automation that scans each item, summarizes it with AI and opens a Jira ticket.
The controller estimates about four hours a week saved (self-reported, June 2025).
Staff review the tickets and act on them.

title: Offshore client accounting redesigned around documented processes, AI workflows and onshore review
problem: Early offshoring was a lift-and-shift of the same process to cheaper labor, and AI tools add another place where client data can travel abroad.
approach: Firms map the as-is process, improve it with automation and AI, and make offshore output a review of work (CohnReznick, Aprio).
An AICPA survey reports 29% of responding firms offshore (independent).
A US lead reviews offshore output and the job manager signs off; consent is captured before return information leaves the US.

title: AI-native provider sells autonomous bookkeeping and close direct to small businesses
problem: Small businesses and startups pay for bookkeeping that is slow and inconsistent, and book catch-up takes weeks (the provider's framing).
approach: Pilot launched its AI Accountant on 4 February 2026, calling it fully autonomous: it onboards, closes historical books and produces statements.
Pilot claims hours, not weeks, and zero human intervention on the normal path (vendor-published).
The business owner reviews flagged items and the audit history, and can adjust transaction-level decisions.

title: AI-native provider supplies platform and leads; a local firm delivers the service
problem: Independent bookkeepers and small firms lack capacity and technology to scale, and AI-native platforms need distribution and local relationships.
approach: Pilot launched a Local Partner Program on 9 December 2025 offering its platform, automation, advisory services, sales tools and matched leads.
Puzzle will work with accounting partners who deliver the service after Accrual's purchase of its firm-facing technology.
No outcome figure is published, and human checkpoints are not described.

title: CLA co-builds a firm-trained AI model with a ledger vendor
problem: CLA's chief executive says AI should not belong only to the biggest firms, and that most vendors CLA evaluated had tacked AI onto decades-old software.
approach: CLA announced on 21 July 2026 it is working with Digits to train a proprietary model on Digits' Firm Model offering.
Digits supplies the platform and training infrastructure; CLA supplies its data. Deployment is planned to thousands of clients over three years.
No outcome figure is published, and human checkpoints are not described.

title: Outcome-based AI ledger pricing: pay only for clients automated 95% or more
problem: Digits' chief executive says that if software does not do the work it should not get paid.
approach: Digits announced (7-8 April 2026) that firms pay for a client only when 95% or more of its transactions are zero-touch.
If staff touch more than 5%, the platform is free for that client; pricing is binary.
Digits cites one customer firm's automation rate moving from about 75% to 98% in 2025 (vendor-published).

title: Client accounting teams advise clients on their own AI adoption
problem: Clients ask their accountant which AI tools to use, what the risks are and how to build dashboards, and some arrive having already used AI.
approach: Teams add AI advisory to the relationship: tool selection, data-protection answers and hands-on demonstrations of dashboards and analysis.
Bonadio's leader says more client AI projects are starting; a San Diego fractional CFO shows clients how to build dashboards.
The accountant owns the advice and the risk framing.
who: Bonadio, a San Diego fractional CFO

title: Idea: control package before agents touch a client's production close
problem: Idea, not a deployment: vendor accuracy claims are not comparable, and agents appear without being listed or owned.
approach: A practitioner article and COSO guidance suggest five written controls: agent inventory, replayable evidence, risk-scaled sign-off gates, SOC mapping, exit thresholds.
A validation period on the client's own data comes first; low-confidence items go to experienced reviewers.
A named owner signs off when an agent is added, changed or retired; a named person can pull the agent.

title: Firm AI policy, approved tools, vendor data terms and change control
problem: About one-third of professionals say they use unsanctioned AI tools, few firms have a written AI policy, and staff can now build unreviewed automations.
approach: The firm names an AI lead, keeps an approved-tool list, defines permitted uses, trains staff and logs how outputs were verified.
It asks providers in writing about data retention and model training, and puts firm-built agents through change management.
One survey finds 21% of firms have an AI policy or strategy (vendor-published); the AI lead approves tools and use cases.
who: Karbon, Thomson Reuters, Journal of Accountancy

title: AI-use disclosure, client consent and client AI terms in engagement letters
problem: Clients ask how their data is used by AI, and no federal law or professional standard says whether or how CPAs must disclose generative AI use.
approach: The firm adds AI-use language to engagement letters or a separate consent: what AI is used for, quality-control steps, third-party disclosure.
Where tax return information is involved it considers the section 7216 consent format and offers a no-AI path for clients who decline.
A partner or counsel approves disclosure and consent wording; staff check which clients declined before opening files.
who: Journal of Accountancy, IESBA, Zuellig Pharma

title: Idea: independence and data-custody screening before selling AI-enabled services to attest clients
problem: Idea, not a deployment: firms that audit some clients and also provide client accounting services must decide which services impair independence for attest clients.
approach: Built from the rules read, the firm checks the client's attest status and regime before offering an AI-enabled service.
Where the Code is silent, it uses the conceptual framework: identify threats, evaluate, apply safeguards, document.
An ethics or independence partner reviews before acceptance; the client's skilled person accepts management responsibility in writing.
